title: The undeclared
hookLine: ten questions the Buddha set aside, and why silence was the answer

cards: A monk named Māluṅkyāputta is sitting alone, and he's had enough. There are questions the Buddha never answers. Is the world eternal, or not?
Is it finite, or infinite? Are the soul and the body the same thing, or different? Does an awakened one exist after death, or not, or both, or neither?
Ten questions in all. So he goes to the Buddha with an ultimatum: answer them, or I'm giving up the training and going home. It's the kind of message you type at two in the morning.

teach.h: DID I EVER PROMISE YOU THAT?
teach.b: First, the Buddha asks a question of his own. Did I ever promise you, come and train with me and I'll answer these? No.
Did you ever say, I'll train only if you do? No. Then who are you, and what are you walking away from?
Suppose a man is shot with an arrow thickly smeared with poison. His friends bring a surgeon. And the man says: don't pull it out until I know who shot me.
Was he a noble, a brahmin, a merchant, a laborer? What was his name, his clan? Tall or short, dark or fair?
What village was he from? What kind of bow was it, what was the string made of, and the feathers on the shaft? That man, the Buddha says, would die before he ever found out.
So the ten questions stay undeclared, avyākata, not answered either way. Not because they're forbidden, and the sutta doesn't call them meaningless.

teach.h: NOT BENEFICIAL, NOT LEADING TO PEACE.
teach.b: Because answering them isn't beneficial, he says. It doesn't lead to letting go, to peace, to awakening. And what has he declared?
This is suffering. This is its arising. This is its ending.
Four things, all about pulling the arrow out.
The sutta ends with a line worth keeping: remember what I've left undeclared as undeclared, and what I've declared as declared. Buddhist schools have gone on discussing the ten questions.
But the silence itself is a teaching. Some questions you can carry for a lifetime without letting them stop you walking.

how: Some Buddhist teachers tell the parable of the poisoned arrow to students who want metaphysical questions settled first, and the ten undeclared questions come up in commentaries and debates across schools.

o: questions too foolish to ask at all
teachings kept secret from new monks

games.q: the poisoned arrow: tap the pairs.

s: the Buddha said the ten questions were meaningless
the sutta says answering them isn't beneficial and doesn't lead to peace.
the Buddha had promised to answer them one day
he asks Māluṅkyāputta whether he ever promised that. he hadn't.
the wounded man in the parable asks what the bowstring was made of
the archer's caste, name, height, village, bow, string, feathers: he'd die first.

games.q: you're shot with a poisoned arrow. the surgeon is ready. what do you do?
o: find out who shot you first
let the surgeon pull it out
ask about the feathers on the arrow
games.why: the man in the parable keeps asking about the archer and dies first. the four things the Buddha declares are all about pulling the arrow out.

practice: Let one big question come up, one you've chewed on, why something happened, what comes after, whether you chose right, and name it once, gently.
Instead of answering, set it down beside you like a closed book and return to the breath. When it taps your shoulder, notice it and come back; it can stay undeclared for now.

wordCard.voice: The undeclared. Ten questions the Buddha set aside, because answering them doesn't pull the arrow out.

orig.note: Pali avyākata (also spelled abyākata): undeclared, left unexplained.

carryVoice: Your line: pull the arrow out. And that's week sixty-five: kukkura, Abhaya, how many feelings, apannaka, before, the earth, and the undeclared. Day four hundred fifty-five.
